title: Seeing Tiny Motion at the Limit of Light
endLine: Wavelength and numerical aperture set resolution; controls test what you see.

scenes.tts: How close can two points get before light blurs them into one? Inside cells, chromosomes part, filaments grow, and tiny motors step along tracks. Light microscopy lets us watch that motion, yet light itself sets a limit.
scenes.caption: How close can two points get before light blurs them into one? Inside cells, chromosomes part, filaments grow, and tiny motors step along tracks. Light microscopy lets us watch that motion, yet light itself sets a limit.
scenes.visual: Carried microscope world: left shows a glass coverslip beneath an objective lens; right shows the live camera view (schematic). Two glowing points on the coverslip drift closer until their ringed spots in the camera view merge into one blur beneath a pulsing question mark.
scenes.narration: How close can two points get before light blurs them into one? Inside cells, chromosomes part, filaments grow, and tiny motors step along tracks. Light microscopy lets us watch that motion, yet light itself sets a limit.

scenes.visual: The same microscope bench stays on screen with gently shimmering light rays inside the objective cone (schematic) while the title 'Seeing Tiny Motion at the Limit of Light' fades in above the stage and settles.

scenes.tts: A lens never images a point as a sharp dot. Light spreads into a bright centre with rings, an Airy pattern. Under the Rayleigh criterion, two points resolve when one centre falls on the other's first dark ring. That smallest separation is resolution.
scenes.caption: A lens never images a point as a sharp dot. Light spreads into a bright centre with rings, an Airy pattern. Under the Rayleigh criterion, two points resolve when one centre falls on the other's first dark ring. That smallest separation is resolution.
scenes.visual: In the right camera view (schematic), one point on the coverslip blooms into a bright centre encircled by a dark ring before the label 'Airy pattern' appears. A second pattern slides in until its centre lands on the first dark ring; a span bar marks 'Resolution'.
scenes.narration: A lens never images a point as a sharp dot. Light spreads into a bright centre with rings, an Airy pattern. Under the Rayleigh criterion, two points resolve when one centre falls on the other's first dark ring. That smallest separation is resolution.

scenes.tts: Resolution depends on emission wavelength lambda, the wavelength a fluorescent label gives off, and numerical aperture, or N A. N A describes the cone of light the objective collects. In an ideal setup, a green label emits at five hundred twenty nanometres. An oil objective, N A one point four zero, resolves two hundred twenty-seven nanometres.
scenes.caption: Resolution depends on emission wavelength λ, the wavelength a fluorescent label gives off, and numerical aperture, or NA. NA describes the cone of light the objective collects. In an ideal setup, a green label emits at 520 nm. An oil objective, NA 1.40, resolves 227 nm.
scenes.visual: On the bench, green rays at λ = 520 nm rise from the coverslip into a wide oil-objective cone labelled 'NA 1.40' (schematic). On the camera view, a 100 nm per pixel grid fades in beneath two Airy patterns separated by 227 nm, resolved at the first dark ring.
scenes.narration: Resolution depends on emission wavelength λ, the wavelength a fluorescent label gives off, and numerical aperture, or NA. NA describes the cone of light the objective collects. In an ideal setup, a green label emits at 520 nm. An oil objective, NA 1.40, resolves 227 nm.

scenes.tts: Keep the same emission and swap objectives. Drop N A to one point zero zero, losing zero point four. The objective collects a narrower light cone. Will the smallest resolvable separation shrink, stay the same, or grow wider?
scenes.caption: Keep the same emission and swap objectives. Drop NA to 1.00, losing 0.4. The objective collects a narrower light cone. Will the smallest resolvable separation shrink, stay the same, or grow wider?
scenes.visual: The oil objective slides aside and a second objective clicks in on the same bench; the green 520 nm light cone visibly narrows from NA 1.40 to NA 1.00 (schematic). The right camera panel masks behind a crisp question card: 'Smaller, same, or wider?'.
scenes.narration: Keep the same emission and swap objectives. Drop NA to 1.00, losing 0.4. The objective collects a narrower light cone. Will the smallest resolvable separation shrink, stay the same, or grow wider?

scenes.visual: The narrowed NA 1.00 light cone shimmers slowly (schematic) while 'Smaller, same, or wider?' remains on screen with a gentle moving progress arc so nothing freezes.

scenes.tts: It grows wider. A narrower cone widens each Airy pattern, pushing resolution to three hundred seventeen point two nanometres. Subtract two hundred twenty-seven from three hundred seventeen point two: about ninety nanometres lost in this model.
scenes.caption: It grows wider. A narrower cone widens each Airy pattern, pushing resolution to 317.2 nm. Subtract 227 from 317.2: about 90 nm lost in this model.
scenes.visual: The question card lifts to reveal wider Airy patterns in the camera view, resolved only at 317.2 nm. Below the gap bar, the subtraction builds as spoken: '317.2 nm − 227 nm ≈ 90 nm lost' (computed from given values), alongside a brief NA 1.40 versus NA 1.00 light-cone comparison.
scenes.narration: It grows wider. A narrower cone widens each Airy pattern, pushing resolution to 317.2 nm. Subtract 227 from 317.2: about 90 nm lost in this model.

scenes.tts: These are ideal values. The instrument's real response to a point, its point-spread function, can be worse with aberrations and thick samples. Suspected missing motor arms in cilia, for example, are confirmed by electron microscopy.
scenes.caption: These are ideal values. The instrument's real response to a point, its point-spread function, can be worse with aberrations and thick samples. Suspected missing motor arms in cilia, for example, are confirmed by electron microscopy.
scenes.visual: A thicker specimen slides onto the coverslip (schematic). On the right camera view, the neat Airy spot warps into a broader, asymmetric blur labelled 'Point-spread function (schematic)'. A side inset shows a greyscale cross-section of a cilium's microtubule bundle with a gap where a motor arm is missing (schematic), labelled 'Electron microscopy'.
scenes.narration: These are ideal values. The instrument's real response to a point, its point-spread function, can be worse with aberrations and thick samples. Suspected missing motor arms in cilia, for example, are confirmed by electron microscopy.

scenes.tts: Seeing motion also takes controls. In a gliding assay, motors stick by their tails to a coverslip under fluorescent filaments. Without A T P, nothing glides; add A T P, and filaments move. And purified systems lack the accessory proteins that change rates inside cells.
scenes.caption: Seeing motion also takes controls. In a gliding assay, motors stick by their tails to a coverslip under fluorescent filaments. Without ATP, nothing glides; add ATP, and filaments move. And purified systems lack the accessory proteins that change rates inside cells.
scenes.visual: On the same glass coverslip (schematic), motor stalks anchor by their tails beneath glowing fluorescent filaments. Under a 'No ATP' tag, the filaments stay still; when 'ATP' pulses in, the filaments glide smoothly across the camera view, while a caution note marks 'Purified vs. cell'.
scenes.narration: Seeing motion also takes controls. In a gliding assay, motors stick by their tails to a coverslip under fluorescent filaments. Without ATP, nothing glides; add ATP, and filaments move. And purified systems lack the accessory proteins that change rates inside cells.

scenes.tts: Light microscopy then unlocked motion directly. In 1984, Mitchison and Kirschner inferred dynamic instability, ends switching between growing and shrinking, from microtubule populations. Microscopy of single ends soon showed switching directly at both ends of purified microtubules.
scenes.caption: Light microscopy then unlocked motion directly. In 1984, Mitchison and Kirschner inferred dynamic instability, ends switching between growing and shrinking, from microtubule populations. Microscopy of single ends soon showed switching directly at both ends of purified microtubules.
scenes.visual: On the coverslip (schematic), a crowd of microtubules appears first, labelled 'Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984: inferred from populations'. The crowd fades to one purified microtubule in the camera view; both ends visibly switch between growing longer and shrinking back, labelled 'single ends: switching seen directly'.
scenes.narration: Light microscopy then unlocked motion directly. In 1984, Mitchison and Kirschner inferred dynamic instability, ends switching between growing and shrinking, from microtubule populations. Microscopy of single ends soon showed switching directly at both ends of purified microtubules.

scenes.tts: Summers and Gibbons studied sea-urchin sperm axonemes, bundles of paired microtubules called doublets. Did the motor dynein slide doublets, or shorten microtubules? They briefly treated axonemes with trypsin, a protein-cutting enzyme, breaking structures that resist sliding. Adding zero point one millimolar A T P sent doublets sliding out under dark-field microscopy. The answer: sliding.
scenes.caption: Summers and Gibbons studied sea-urchin sperm axonemes, bundles of paired microtubules called doublets. Did the motor dynein slide doublets, or shorten microtubules? They briefly treated axonemes with trypsin, a protein-cutting enzyme, breaking structures that resist sliding. Adding 0.1 mM ATP sent doublets sliding out under dark-field microscopy. The answer: sliding.
scenes.visual: On the coverslip (schematic), a bright bundle of sea-urchin sperm axoneme doublets glows against a black dark-field background. As 'trypsin' breaks cross-links and '0.1 mM ATP' pulses in, groups of doublets telescope smoothly out of the bundle in the camera view, labelled 'Summers and Gibbons'.
scenes.narration: Summers and Gibbons studied sea-urchin sperm axonemes, bundles of paired microtubules called doublets. Did the motor dynein slide doublets, or shorten microtubules? They briefly treated axonemes with trypsin, a protein-cutting enzyme, breaking structures that resist sliding. Adding 0.1 mM ATP sent doublets sliding out under dark-field microscopy. The answer: sliding.

scenes.tts: Tracking one dye even revealed motor steps. Kinesin one walks hand over hand along microtubule binding sites eight nanometres apart. Its cargo moves eight nanometres per step. The rear head swings past the front, so it moves two spacings: two times eight is sixteen. In a 2004 imaging study, a dye on one head moved about seventeen nanometres.
scenes.caption: Tracking one dye even revealed motor steps. Kinesin-1 walks hand over hand along microtubule binding sites 8 nm apart. Its cargo moves 8 nm per step. The rear head swings past the front, so it moves two spacings: 2 × 8 = 16. In a 2004 imaging study, a dye on one head moved about 17 nm.
scenes.visual: On the coverslip (schematic), a two-headed kinesin-1 motor walks hand over hand along a microtubule with binding-site ticks 8 nm apart. The cargo shifts 8 nm per step; the rear head swings past the front head across two ticks while '2 × 8 = 16 nm' writes on screen as spoken. A glowing dye spot on one head then hops about 17 nm, labelled '2004 imaging study'.
scenes.narration: Tracking one dye even revealed motor steps. Kinesin-1 walks hand over hand along microtubule binding sites 8 nm apart. Its cargo moves 8 nm per step. The rear head swings past the front, so it moves two spacings: 2 × 8 = 16. In a 2004 imaging study, a dye on one head moved about 17 nm.

scenes.visual: The microscope bench fades softly behind the clean end card displaying only: 'Wavelength and numerical aperture set resolution; controls test what you see.' with subtle ambient shimmer.
